As an imagined beast, the manticore has been found in literature as early as the 5th and 4th century BC. In his *Indica*, the Greek physician Ctesias, working for the Persian court describes the Manticore as a beast with red skin, as large as a lion, possessing three rows of teeth, a human-like face and the tail of a scorpion. Later writers would quote Ctesias’ description of the Manticore adding emphasis on its dietary habits, including that it ate men. Though it is likely that many of these descriptions were of predatory animals passed by word of mouth until they reached the Persian king’s court, what is even more important is the way in which these descriptions begin to stand in for imageries of evil in the Medieval literature and specifically the kinds of evil they begin the represent.
